diag_intro: Select the symptoms you observe in your pigs to narrow down potential diseases.
diag_no_matches: No strong matches found based on current symptoms. Please consult a veterinarian for a thorough checkup.
diag_other_symptoms_to_lookout: Other symptoms to look out for
dis_aflatoxicosis_desc: Toxin poisoning from moldy grains or feed causing liver damage and jaundice.
dis_aflatoxicosis_prev: Avoid feeding moldy feed, store grains in dry conditions, and use toxin binders.
dis_anaplasmosis_desc: Tick-borne bacterial infection causing anemia, fever, and jaundice.
dis_anaplasmosis_prev: Implement vector and tick control programs.
dis_anemia_desc: Common in indoor piglets without iron supplements.
dis_anthrax_desc: Serious bacterial disease that can affect humans.
dis_ascaris_desc: Internal parasite causing lung and liver damage.
dis_asf_desc: A highly contagious and deadly viral disease prevalent in West Africa. No vaccine exists.
dis_asf_prev: Strict biosecurity and restrict farm access.
dis_babesiosis_desc: Tick-transmitted blood parasite causing high fever, anemia, and dark urine.
dis_babesiosis_prev: Control ticks using acaricides and keep pens free of vegetation.
dis_biotin_deficiency_desc: Nutritional deficiency causing cracked hooves, skin lesions, and lameness.
dis_biotin_deficiency_prev: Supplement diet with biotin and avoid rough, wet concrete floors.
dis_bvdv_pig_desc: Bovine Viral Diarrhea virus infection from contact with cattle, causing abortion.
dis_bvdv_pig_prev: Keep pigs separate from cattle and sheep, and restrict cross-species contacts.
dis_c_difficile_desc: Bacterial infection in newborn piglets causing watery diarrhea and bloating.
dis_c_difficile_prev: Clean and disinfect farrowing pens thoroughly and ensure early colostrum.
dis_cassava_poisoning_desc: Cyanide poisoning from raw or improperly processed cassava roots or peels.
dis_cassava_poisoning_prev: Peel, boil, sun-dry, or ferment cassava before feeding.
dis_clostridial_desc: Bacterial infection causing severe gut damage.
dis_cold_stress_desc: Severe body cooling in piglets, causing shivering and high mortality.
dis_cold_stress_prev: Provide heat lamps, creep boxes, and keep farrowing area dry and draft-free.
dis_congenital_tremor_desc: Neurological condition in newborn piglets causing severe trembling.
dis_congenital_tremor_prev: Avoid using semen from affected boars and minimize sow stress during gestation.
dis_csf_desc: Highly contagious viral disease similar to ASF.
dis_cysticercosis_desc: Larval stage of human tapeworm in pig muscle.
dis_demodectic_mange_desc: Microscopic skin mite causing scaly spots and small pustules.
dis_demodectic_mange_prev: Improve herd nutrition, isolate affected pigs, and apply acaricides.
dis_ear_biting_desc: Abnormal behavior where pigs bite ears of pen-mates, causing necrosis.
dis_ear_biting_prev: Reduce crowding, improve ventilation, and provide enrichment like chains.
dis_ear_necrosis_desc: Often caused by stress, overcrowding, or infection.
dis_ear_necrosis_prev: Reduce density and treat secondary infection.
dis_edema_desc: Caused by E. coli toxins in weaned piglets.
dis_emcv_desc: Rodent-borne viral infection causing sudden heart failure and abortion.
dis_emcv_prev: Implement strict rodent control and protect feed from contamination.
dis_endocarditis_desc: Heart valve infection causing heart failure and sudden death during stress.
dis_endocarditis_prev: Promptly treat joint-ill and wounds, and select against susceptible genetics.
dis_ergotism_desc: Fungal poisoning from ergot-infected cereal grains, causing tissue necrosis.
dis_ergotism_prev: Screen feed grains for dark ergot bodies and replace contaminated feed.
dis_erysipelas_desc: Bacterial infection causing distinct skin lesions and arthritis.
dis_fascioliasis_desc: Parasitic fluke affecting the liver, common in wet or swampy pastures.
dis_fascioliasis_prev: Prevent pigs from grazing in swampy areas and control mud snails.
dis_fmd_desc: Viral disease causing blisters on the mouth and feet.
dis_foot_rot_desc: Bacterial infection entering hoof injuries, causing rotting and lameness.
dis_foot_rot_prev: Repair rough concrete, keep floors dry, and use foot baths if needed.
dis_gastric_torsion_desc: Sudden bloating and twisting of the stomach, leading to rapid death.
dis_gastric_torsion_prev: Avoid feeding large meals after long fasts and divide daily feed into portions.
dis_glassers_desc: Causes inflammation of membranes around heart, lungs, joints.
dis_gossypol_toxicity_desc: Poisoning from feeding raw or excess cottonseed meal, causing respiratory distress.
dis_gossypol_toxicity_prev: Limit cottonseed meal in diet and use iron sulfate to neutralize gossypol.
dis_greasy_pig_desc: Bacterial infection causing greasy skin lesions.
dis_heat_stroke_desc: Overheating due to poor ventilation or shade.
dis_hydatid_disease_desc: Parasitic larval infection causing fluid-filled cysts in organs.
dis_hydatid_disease_prev: Deworm farm dogs regularly and prevent them from eating raw pig organs.
dis_hyostrongylosis_desc: Stomach worm infection causing gastritis, anemia, and weight loss.
dis_hyostrongylosis_prev: Rotate pastures, keep housing dry, and implement a deworming schedule.
dis_ileitis_desc: Bacterial infection of the small intestine.
dis_iron_toxicity_desc: Can occur if iron is injected into Vit E deficient piglets.
dis_kidney_worms_desc: Internal parasite affecting kidneys and liver.
dis_mange_desc: Parasitic skin disease causing extreme discomfort.
dis_mma_desc: Mastitis, metritis, and agalactia causing fever and lack of milk in sows after farrowing.
dis_mma_prev: Maintain strict farrowing pen hygiene and ensure adequate sow nutrition.
dis_mycoplasma_arthritis_desc: Bacterial infection causing swollen joints, lameness, and leg weakness.
dis_mycoplasma_arthritis_prev: Improve housing conditions, reduce stocking density, and treat early.
dis_navel_bleeding_desc: Excessive bleeding from the umbilical cord in newborn piglets.
dis_navel_bleeding_prev: Tie umbilical cords at birth and avoid feeding mycotoxin-contaminated feed to sows.
dis_navel_ill_desc: Infection of the umbilical cord at birth.
dis_navel_ill_prev: Iodine dip at birth and sanitation.
dis_necrotic_enteritis_desc: Bacterial toxin disease causing severe bloody diarrhea and high mortality in piglets.
dis_necrotic_enteritis_prev: Vaccinate sows before farrowing and maintain absolute pen hygiene.
dis_oesophagostomiasis_desc: Intestinal parasite causing nodules in the gut wall, leading to thin sows.
dis_oesophagostomiasis_prev: Regular pen sanitation and routine use of broad-spectrum anthelmintics.
dis_parakeratosis_desc: Nutritional disease causing severe crusty, thickened skin lesions.
dis_parakeratosis_prev: Ensure balanced calcium-to-zinc ratio in feed and provide zinc supplements.
dis_pcv2_desc: Causes wasting and respiratory issues in growers.
dis_ped_desc: Similar to TGE, highly fatal to neonates.
dis_phe_desc: Acute bloody diarrhea and sudden death in grower/finisher pigs.
dis_phe_prev: Maintain good sanitation and use appropriate antibiotics under vet guidance.
dis_photosensitization_desc: Severe sunburn-like reaction in light-skinned pigs after eating specific plants.
dis_photosensitization_prev: Provide shade, remove sensitizing weeds, and keep pigs indoors.
dis_pityriasis_rosea_desc: Non-contagious skin condition in young pigs forming ring-like crusts.
dis_pityriasis_rosea_prev: Usually self-resolving; maintain clean, dry bedding and reduce stress.
dis_pneumonia_desc: Chronic respiratory disease leading to poor growth.
dis_polyserositis_desc: Fibrinous inflammation of lung, heart, and joint surfaces in weaners.
dis_polyserositis_prev: Minimize weaning stress, avoid mixing litters, and ventilate properly.
dis_pox_desc: Viral skin disease, often spread by lice.
dis_ppv_desc: Common cause of reproductive failure in gilts.
dis_prdc_desc: Mixed viral and bacterial respiratory infection causing coughing and poor growth.
dis_prdc_prev: Improve ventilation, avoid overcrowding, and control primary viruses.
dis_prrs_desc: Causes respiratory failure and reproductive issues.
dis_pseudorabies_desc: Viral disease affecting nervous and respiratory systems.
dis_pwd_desc: Bacterial diarrhea in piglets shortly after weaning, causing dehydration.
dis_pwd_prev: Reduce weaning stress, maintain high sanitation, and provide clean drinking water.
dis_rabies_desc: Fatal viral disease usually from bites.
dis_rabies_prev: Vaccination of pets and wildlife control.
dis_rectal_prolapse_desc: Often follows coughing, diarrhea, or cold stress.
dis_rhinitis_desc: Causes distortion of the snout and respiratory issues.
dis_salmonella_septicemia_desc: Severe bloodstream salmonella infection causing purple skin and rapid death.
dis_salmonella_septicemia_prev: Isolate sick pigs, medicate water, and maintain strict biosecurity.
dis_salmonellosis_desc: Bacterial infection causing severe gut issues.
dis_salt_poisoning_desc: Caused by lack of water followed by over-consumption.
dis_shoulder_ulcers_desc: Pressure sores on the shoulders of thin sows housed on hard concrete.
dis_shoulder_ulcers_prev: Provide soft bedding, keep sows in good body condition, and use rubber mats.
dis_sow_hysteria_desc: Behavioral disorder where farrowing sows become aggressive and bite piglets.
dis_sow_hysteria_prev: Provide a quiet farrowing environment, supervise gilts, and use sedatives if needed.
dis_spirochetal_colitis_desc: Mild diarrheal disease in growing pigs, causing poor weight gain.
dis_spirochetal_colitis_prev: Sanitize feeding troughs and treat affected pigs with antibiotics.
dis_splayleg_desc: Piglets born unable to stand with hind legs.
dis_strongyloidiasis_desc: Intestinal threadworm causing severe diarrhea and mortality in piglets.
dis_strongyloidiasis_prev: Keep farrowing crates dry and clean, and deworm sows before farrowing.
dis_sweet_potato_toxicity_desc: Poisoning from moldy sweet potatoes, causing severe respiratory distress.
dis_sweet_potato_toxicity_prev: Discard damaged or moldy sweet potatoes; feed only healthy tubers.
dis_teschen_desc: Viral infection of the nervous system.
dis_tetanus_desc: Bacterial toxin affecting the nervous system.
dis_tge_desc: Viral disease with high mortality in young piglets.
dis_thorny_headed_worm_desc: Parasitic worm acquired by eating beetles, causing gut perforation.
dis_thorny_headed_worm_prev: Avoid free-range rearing on beetle-infested soils and use dewormers.
dis_trichinellosis_desc: Zoonotic parasitic disease from eating raw meat scraps, causing muscle stiffness.
dis_trichinellosis_prev: Do not feed raw swill, boil food scraps for 30 minutes, and control rodents.
dis_trypanosomiasis_desc: Protozoan disease spread by tsetse flies.
dis_ulcers_desc: Caused by fine feed or stress.
dis_vulvovaginitis_desc: Caused by estrogenic fungal toxins in feed.
dis_whipworms_desc: Internal parasite in the large intestine.

guide_breeding_step1_desc: Look for standing reflex, swollen vulva, and vocalizations. Record natural service or AI with boar tag details.
guide_breeding_step1_tip: Best practice is to serve the sow twice: 12 hours apart during peak standing heat.
guide_breeding_step2_desc: SmartSwine automatically schedules repeat heat checks at 18-24 days and farrowing alerts around 110-114 days.
guide_breeding_step2_tip: Check for return to heat around Day 21. If sow shows standing heat, re-service immediately.
guide_breeding_step3_desc: Disinfect farrowing crates and move pregnant sows 4 to 5 days before expected due date. Prepare heat lamps for piglets.
guide_breeding_step3_tip: Keep the piglet creep area warm (30-32°C) to prevent hypothermia in newborns.
guide_breeding_step4_desc: Log Born Alive, Stillborns, Mummies, and Total Litter Birth Weight to evaluate sow maternal performance.
guide_breeding_step4_tip: Administer iron injections and clip needle teeth within 24-48 hours of farrowing.
guide_breeding_subtitle: Track sow heat cycles, serve dates, 114-day gestation, and farrowing litters.
guide_feed_step1_desc: Go to 'Feed' and open the 'Feed Formulation' tool to create or adjust custom feeding rations.
guide_feed_step1_tip: Check ingredient market prices beforehand to identify the most cost-effective local protein and energy sources.
guide_feed_step2_desc: Choose the target pig stage (Creep, Starter, Grower, Finisher, Gestating Sow, Lactating Sow) to load standard nutrient requirements.
guide_feed_step2_tip: Grower pigs require higher crude protein (16-18%) than gestating sows (12-14%).
guide_feed_step3_desc: Add ingredients such as Maize, Soya Meal, Wheat Bran, Fishmeal, and Premix. Balance percentages until nutrient bars turn green.
guide_feed_step3_tip: Ensure the Calcium to Phosphorus (Ca:P) ratio stays between 1.2:1 and 1.6:1 for healthy bone development.
guide_feed_step4_desc: Save your balanced recipe for quick access, or log a mixed batch to automatically update feed inventory.
guide_feed_step4_tip: Mix feed in uniform batches and store in dry, elevated pallets to prevent aflatoxin and spoilage.
guide_feed_subtitle: Design cost-effective, nutritionally complete diets for every production stage.
guide_finances_step1_desc: Log all farm expenditures categorized by Feed, Veterinary, Labor, Utilities, and Maintenance.
guide_finances_step1_tip: Log expenses as soon as purchases occur so cost analytics stay up to date.
guide_finances_step2_desc: Record income from live animal sales, slaughtered carcasses, breeding stock, or organic manure.
guide_finances_step2_tip: Record both live weight and final price per kg to track realized market margins.
guide_finances_step3_desc: Review COP per kg and Finisher Breakeven price to ensure each transaction generates healthy profit.
guide_finances_step3_tip: Feed should ideally represent 65-75% of your total production cost. Minimize feed wastage.
guide_finances_subtitle: Track expenses, sales revenue, and calculate cost of production per kg.
guide_health_step1_desc: Use the Disease Finder tool to match observed clinical signs (coughing, diarrhea, lesions) with common swine conditions.
guide_health_step1_tip: Isolate sick animals immediately into quarantine pens before beginning treatment.
guide_health_step2_desc: Record antibiotic or antiparasitic treatments and strictly note meat withdrawal days.
guide_health_step2_tip: Never market or slaughter an animal before the full meat withdrawal window expires.
guide_health_step3_desc: Maintain footbaths with disinfectant, control farm visitors, sanitize vehicles, and quarantine new stock for 30 days.
guide_health_step3_tip: Biosecurity is 10 times cheaper than treating a disease outbreak.
guide_health_subtitle: Identify symptoms, follow treatment protocols, and maintain strict biosecurity.
guide_herd_step1_desc: Access 'Herd Data' from the main dashboard or drawer menu to view your entire herd registry.
guide_herd_step1_tip: You can filter herd records by status (Active, Sold, Cull) using the status tabs.
guide_herd_step2_desc: Tap the '+' floating button. Fill in essential information: Tag ID, Breed, Sex, Birth Date, and Pen location.
guide_herd_step2_tip: Assign clear, standardized tag IDs (e.g., SOW-001, BOAR-01) for easier farm-wide tracking.
guide_herd_step3_desc: Open any animal's profile card to log regular scale weights, vaccinations, deworming, or medical treatments.
guide_herd_step3_tip: Regular weighing helps calculate precise Average Daily Gain (ADG) and detect illness early.
guide_herd_step4_desc: Group growing pigs into designated pens or batch groups to accurately monitor pen density and feed consumption.
guide_herd_step4_tip: Avoid overcrowded pens to prevent biting behaviors and ensure uniform animal growth.
guide_herd_subtitle: Register animals, manage ear tags, assign pens, and track lineage.
guide_hr_step1_desc: Register workers, farm managers, and consulting vets with role-specific access permissions.
guide_hr_step1_tip: Restricting financial access to Admins and Managers keeps sensitive records safe.
guide_hr_step2_desc: Delegate daily routines such as pen feeding, waterer cleaning, farrowing watches, and heat detection.
guide_hr_step2_tip: Clear task checklists prevent missed feedings or delayed medication rounds.
guide_hr_step3_desc: Log salary payments, bonuses, and deductions to maintain a transparent, organized payroll history.
guide_hr_step3_tip: Always include notes on performance bonuses or salary advances for audit clarity.
guide_hr_subtitle: Manage workers, assign daily tasks, track attendance, and log payroll.
guide_intro_desc: Step-by-step interactive workflows to streamline herd health, feed formulation, breeding cycles, financials, and staff management.
guide_offline_step1_desc: Record animal additions, feed logs, breeding services, and treatments even without Wi-Fi or cellular signal.
guide_offline_step1_tip: All changes are saved locally to your device's secure offline database.
guide_offline_step2_desc: When internet connectivity is restored, all offline updates automatically synchronize with the cloud database.
guide_offline_step2_tip: Check the offline banner at the top of the screen to verify your current connection status.
guide_offline_subtitle: Work seamlessly without internet in remote pens; sync automatically when reconnected.
guide_weight_step1_desc: When a scale is unavailable, measure heart girth behind the front legs and length from ears to tail base.
guide_weight_step1_tip: Keep the measuring tape snug against the pig's skin without compressing the flesh.
guide_weight_step2_desc: SmartSwine computes ADG between weighings to monitor growth trajectory against standard benchmarks.
guide_weight_step2_tip: Target ADG for commercial growers is 650g - 850g/day under good nutrition.
guide_weight_step3_desc: View projected market slaughter date (target 90-100kg) to plan feed budgets and advance buyer sales.
guide_weight_step3_tip: Plan your finisher sales in advance to lock in favorable buyer agreements.
guide_weight_subtitle: Estimate pig weights, track growth velocity, and forecast slaughter dates.

tip_100_content: Keep clear emergency contacts and instructions posted near the entrance for power outages, water cuts, or fire hazards.
tip_10_content: Group piglets of similar sizes together at weaning. This prevents larger piglets from dominant behavior and hoarding feed.
tip_11_content: Feed a cheap, homemade electrolyte solution (5 tablespoons sugar, 1/2 tablespoon salt in 5 liters clean water) during the first 3 days of weaning to combat stress.
tip_12_content: If feeding kitchen waste to weaners, always boil it for at least 30 minutes to kill viruses and bacteria before feeding.
tip_13_content: Feed the same starter diet for 5 days after weaning before slowly mixing in grower feed over a 7-day period to prevent diarrhea.
tip_14_content: Provide a thick layer of dry straw, wood shavings, or dry grass in the sleeping area to keep weaned piglets warm without using expensive heaters.
tip_15_content: Ensure all piglets can eat at the same time by providing long, low wooden or concrete feed troughs (about 15-20cm of trough space per piglet).
tip_16_content: Hang split green banana stems in the weaning pen. Piglets chew on them, which keeps them occupied and prevents tail-biting.
tip_17_content: Put a clean shovel of fresh, red clay soil (from a clean area) in the farrowing/weaning pen. Piglets eat it to get natural iron and minerals.
tip_18_content: Place water troughs or nipple drinkers low enough (back-height of the smallest piglet) so all weaned pigs can drink easily.
tip_19_content: Open the partition between two farrowing pens a week before weaning to let piglets socialize, reducing fighting when grouped later.
tip_1_content: High quality feed is essential. Ensure pigs have constant access to fresh water and balanced nutrition tailored to their growth stage.
tip_20_content: Boil agricultural byproducts like yam peels, cassava peels, and potato vines to destroy natural toxins and improve digestibility.
tip_21_content: Supplement commercial feed by growing high-protein forage crops like Moringa, Azolla, or sweet potato leaves on the farm.
tip_22_content: Limit gestating sows to 2-2.5 kg of feed per day to prevent them from becoming overweight, which causes difficult births.
tip_23_content: Mix cheap local fiber sources like rice bran, wheat bran, or copra meal into sow gestation feed to keep them full and calm.
tip_24_content: Use recycled plastic barrels or drums fitted with nipple drinkers as a cheap, clean water system for all pig pens.
tip_25_content: Store feed bags on wooden pallets off the concrete floor and away from walls to prevent dampness and mold growth.
tip_26_content: Boil hotel or kitchen food waste for 30 minutes to destroy African Swine Fever and Foot-and-Mouth disease viruses.
tip_27_content: Use wet brewer's grain as a cheap feed base, but limit it to 30-40% of the ration and feed it fresh to avoid mold poisoning.
tip_28_content: Place small pieces of wood charcoal in grower pens. Pigs chew it to help bind stomach toxins and reduce diarrhea.
tip_29_content: Feed lactating sows 3 to 4 small meals throughout the day (instead of one big meal) to encourage them to eat more and produce more milk.
tip_2_content: Biosecurity is key. Limit visitors, provide footbaths, and maintain a strict vaccination schedule with your veterinarian.
tip_30_content: When mixing feed on-farm, mix micro-ingredients (vitamins, salt, minerals) into a small batch of maize first before blending into the main pile.
tip_31_content: Limit Leucaena (ipil-ipil) leaf meal to under 5% of feed, as it contains mimosine which can cause hair loss and reproductive failure.
tip_32_content: Feed thin sows extra feed during mid-gestation, and reduce feed for fat sows to maintain a healthy body condition.
tip_33_content: Clean drinking troughs daily. If the water looks dirty or smells bad to you, it is not safe for your pigs.
tip_34_content: Bring the sow in heat to the boar's pen for breeding, rather than letting the boar run loose in the sow herd.
tip_35_content: Test for heat by pressing your hands firmly on the sow's back; if she stands completely still and stiffens her ears, she is ready to mate.
tip_36_content: Scrub farrowing pens with a mixture of agricultural lime and water (whitewashing) to disinfect walls and floors cheaply.
tip_37_content: Dry wet newborn piglets immediately using clean, dry sacks or rags to prevent chilling and respiratory sickness.
tip_38_content: If iron injections are unavailable, rub a clean soil and iron-sulfate paste on the sow's teats daily so piglets ingest iron while nursing.
tip_3_content: Keep newborn piglets warm and ensure they receive colostrum within the first hours of birth to build immunity.
tip_40_content: Use a simple wooden box with a small light bulb or warm bedding (like dry straw) to keep piglets warm in the creep area.
tip_41_content: Wash the sow's udder and teats with clean warm water and a mild disinfectant before she farrows to protect newborn piglets.
tip_42_content: Hand-express colostrum from the sow's teats and feed it to weak piglets using a clean syringe or spoon.
tip_43_content: Mark the breeding date on a calendar; pregnancy lasts 114 days (3 months, 3 weeks, 3 days), allowing you to prepare the farrowing pen.
tip_44_content: Keep replacement gilts from mothers that had large litter sizes, good milk production, and calm mothering instincts.
tip_45_content: Walk a mature boar past the gilt pens daily to encourage them to come into heat earlier and show clear heat signs.
tip_46_content: Place a bucket of clean water close to the farrowing sow's head so she can drink without getting up.
tip_47_content: Wait until a gilt is at least 8 months old and on her second or third heat cycle before mating her to ensure a larger first litter.
tip_48_content: Keep newly purchased pigs in a separate pen at least 20 meters away from your main herd for 30 days to check for sickness.
tip_49_content: Place a shallow plastic tub or half-cut tire filled with water and disinfectant (like chlorine or agricultural lime) at the farm gate.
tip_4_content: Proper manure handling prevents odor and disease. Consider composting or using waste as fertilizer for crops.
tip_50_content: Keep growers, finishers, and breeding sows in separate pens to prevent older pigs from passing chronic diseases to younger ones.
tip_51_content: Do not allow visitors (especially other pig buyers or farmers) inside your pig pens. Discuss business outside the pen area.
tip_52_content: Build a simple fence (using bamboo, wood, or wire mesh) around the piggery to keep out stray dogs, wild pigs, and neighbors.
tip_53_content: Store used needles in a sealed plastic bottle or container before burying or disposing of them safely to prevent accidental injuries.
tip_54_content: Never allow pig buyers to drive their trucks near your pig pens. Load sold pigs at the farm gate or perimeter fence.
tip_55_content: Feed crushed papaya seeds or pumpkin seeds to grower pigs as a cheap, natural remedy to help reduce internal worms.
tip_56_content: If docking tails, disinfect the cutting tool in boiling water or alcohol between piglets to prevent infection.
tip_57_content: Clean and spray the pig pens weekly with a cheap, effective disinfectant solution, ensuring pigs are moved or floors dry quickly.
tip_58_content: Ensure your herd boar is vaccinated and de-wormed regularly, as he can spread infections to all breeding sows.
tip_59_content: Set aside one isolated, dry, warm pen at the far end of the farm to treat sick pigs away from the healthy herd.
tip_5_content: Track growth, health, and financials meticulously to identify trends and improve farm profitability.
tip_60_content: Bury dead pigs at least 2 meters deep, far away from water sources, and cover the carcass with agricultural lime before refilling the soil.
tip_61_content: Provide at least 1 square meter of space per finisher pig to reduce fighting, stress, and skin lesions.
tip_62_content: Design pig houses with open sides (using wire mesh or bamboo slats) to allow natural breeze to blow through and remove odors.
tip_63_content: Paint metal roofs with white paint or cover them with palm leaves or thatch to reduce heat inside the pig house during hot days.
tip_64_content: When laying concrete floors, scratch the surface with a broom to create small grooves so pigs do not slip and injure their legs.
tip_65_content: Use dry sawdust or wood shavings on solid floors to absorb moisture, keeping pigs dry and reducing clean-up labor.
tip_66_content: Clean manure out of pens daily. High ammonia gas levels (indicated by burning eyes or strong smell) can damage pigs' lungs.
tip_67_content: For pigs kept outdoors or in open dirt pens, provide a shaded mud wallow to help them cool down in hot weather.
tip_68_content: Wash and scrub wooden or concrete feed troughs weekly to prevent soured feed from causing stomach upsets.
tip_69_content: Hang plastic bottles filled with small stones or rubber tires in the pens to give pigs something to play with, reducing fighting.
tip_6_content: Wean piglets at 28 to 35 days instead of earlier. This allows piglets to grow stronger and adapt to solid feed using simple farm resources.
tip_70_content: Plant leafy trees on the east and west sides of the pig house to provide natural shade and block hot afternoon sun.
tip_71_content: Slope the concrete floor slightly (about 2-3%) toward the drainage channel so the resting area stays dry while the dunging area is wet.
tip_72_content: Provide individual gestation pens or partitions using sturdy local timber to protect pregnant sows from being bullied by others.
tip_73_content: Use coconut leaves, palm leaves, or straw thatch under corrugated metal roofs as a cheap way to insulate the building.
tip_74_content: Use split bamboo or wooden poles bound with wire as sturdy, cheap fencing materials for outdoor pig runs.
tip_75_content: Pile pig manure in a designated dry corner, cover it with banana leaves or plastic, and turn it weekly with a shovel to make compost.
tip_76_content: Install a simple, low-cost plastic tubular biogas digester to treat pig manure, producing free cooking gas for the household.
tip_77_content: Collect wastewater from pen washing in a storage pit, dilute it with clean water, and use it to water bananas or crops.
tip_78_content: Spread a layer of dry sawdust on manure channels to absorb odors and dry out waste, making it easier to shovel.
tip_79_content: Install simple gutters (using halved bamboo or cheap PVC pipes) to divert rainwater away from manure pits and pens.
tip_7_content: Reduce weaning stress by moving the sow out of the farrowing pen and leaving the piglets in their familiar environment for the first week.
tip_80_content: If burial is not possible, build a simple compost bin using wooden pallets to compost dead piglets in dry sawdust.
tip_81_content: Build a small concrete settling box in the drain channel to catch solid manure before the wastewater enters a pond or garden.
tip_82_content: Plant fast-growing shrubs or trees (like banana plants or lemongrass) around the piggery to block wind and reduce smells.
tip_83_content: Build a simple raised wooden or concrete platform to sun-dry solid manure before packing it in bags for sale as fertilizer.
tip_84_content: Clear drainage channels daily using a simple scraper to prevent stagnant water, mosquito breeding, and bad smells.
tip_85_content: Partner with nearby vegetable or crop farmers to exchange pig manure for crop waste, straw, or grain byproducts.
tip_86_content: Spread composted pig manure onto crop soils at least 2 weeks before planting, rather than directly on growing vegetables.
tip_87_content: Keep manure storage piles covered with a tarpaulin or thatch roof to prevent rain from washing away valuable crop nutrients.
tip_88_content: Use a simple square piece of plywood or plastic (sorting board) to guide and move pigs gently, rather than using sticks.
tip_89_content: Walk slowly through the pens every morning and evening. Observe if all pigs stand up, are active, and look interested in feed.
tip_8_content: Block cold winds in the nursery pen by installing temporary curtains or wooden boards up to piglet-height (about 50cm).
tip_90_content: Use a simple V-notch tool to notch piglet ears for identification, disinfecting the tool in alcohol after each piglet.
tip_91_content: Estimate a pig's weight using a simple sewing tape measure (measure heart girth and length, then calculate weight) if scales are too expensive.
tip_92_content: Castrate male piglets before they are 7 days old. At this age, the procedure is fast, heals quickly, and causes minimal pain.
tip_93_content: Move pigs to market during the early morning or evening when it is cool, and shade the transport vehicle with coconut leaves.
tip_94_content: Keep a small, cheap notebook in the barn to write down breeding dates, farrowing dates, and treatments for each sow.
tip_95_content: Write down simple daily farm rules (like washing hands, cleaning troughs, checking water) on a board near the barn entrance.
tip_96_content: Teach children or helpers on the farm to handle pigs gently, avoiding kicking or tail-pulling, which makes pigs wild and dangerous.
tip_97_content: Store feed in sealed plastic buckets or oil drums to prevent attracting mice, rats, and snakes to the farm.
tip_98_content: Check water drinkers twice daily by pressing them with your finger to ensure water flows freely and is not clogged with dirt.
tip_99_content: Cull sows that fail to get pregnant after two breeding attempts with a proven boar, or those that have small litters (under 6 piglets).

emergency_containment_protocol_steps:
1. 🔒 Immediate Quarantine: Seal affected pen immediately; restrict personnel access.
2. 🚫 Movement Freeze: Cease all live pig, pork, feed, and manure shipments off-farm.
3. 🧼 Disinfect: Deploy boot baths & tyre dips with Virkon S or 2% caustic soda.
4. 📞 Mandatory Reporting: Contact your District Veterinary Officer immediately.
5. ⚠️ No Slaughter: Do not slaughter sick or suspect animals for meat.
bio_proto_asf: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY QUARANTINE: African Swine Fever is a lethal, legally notifiable virus. 1) Lock down farm gates immediately. 2) Stop all movement of pigs, vehicles, feed, and manure. 3) Disinfect all boot baths and tyres with Virkon S or 2% caustic soda. 4) Contact your District/National Veterinary Officer immediately.
bio_proto_fmd: NOTIFIABLE EPIDEMIC ALERT: Foot-and-Mouth Disease spreads rapidly through aerosols and equipment. 1) Quarantine suspect pen immediately. 2) No live pigs or personnel movement off-site. 3) Setup tyre baths and boot dips with approved disinfectant. 4) Notify livestock authorities immediately.
bio_proto_csf: NOTIFIABLE DISEASE ALERT: Classical Swine Fever (Hog Cholera). 1) Restrict pen access and isolate suspect animals. 2) Halt all pig sales and shipments. 3) Wear dedicated boots/overalls. 4) Report to official state veterinary services immediately.
bio_proto_anthrax: DANGER - ZOONOTIC EMERGENCY: Bacillus anthracis can infect humans. 1) DO NOT OPEN CARCASSES (exposure to air causes resistant spores). 2) Isolate surviving pigs. 3) Wear full PPE. 4) Call veterinary authorities for safe incineration or deep burial with quicklime.
bio_proto_pseudorabies: NOTIFIABLE HERPESVIRUS ALERT: Pseudorabies / Aujeszky's causes severe neurological fatality in piglets. 1) Strict pen quarantine. 2) Control wild animals and rodents. 3) Notify state veterinary authorities immediately.
bio_proto_rabies: FATAL ZOONOTIC ALERT: Rabies transmits to humans through saliva and bites. 1) DO NOT HANDLE PIG WITH BARE HANDS. 2) Secure pen tightly. 3) Alert veterinary and public health authorities immediately.
bio_proto_vesicular_stomatitis: REPORTABLE VESICULAR LESION ALERT: Vesicular Stomatitis is clinically indistinguishable from Foot and Mouth Disease. 1) Isolate infected pigs immediately. 2) Wear protective gloves. 3) Report to state veterinarian for lab differential diagnosis.
bio_proto_senecavirus: REPORTABLE VESICULAR DISEASE: Senecavirus A lesions are clinically indistinguishable from Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD). 1) Quarantine pen immediately. 2) Restrict off-farm movement. 3) Notify livestock veterinary authorities for mandatory differential PCR testing.
bio_proto_svd: REPORTABLE VESICULAR DISEASE: Swine Vesicular Disease (SVD). 1) Strict isolation of infected animals. 2) Restrict all vehicle and visitor movements. 3) Report to state animal health department immediately.
